questions.q: What does a change impact assessment add on top of the impact analysis from Lesson 14?
options: It formalizes impact analysis into a repeatable, documented process every meaningful change goes through
It replaces the need to trace lineage at all
It only applies to changes that affect the user interface
It is performed only after a change has already shipped
questions.explain: A change impact assessment takes the one-off downstream walk from Lesson 14 and formalizes it into a process with defined stages, performed before a change ships.

questions.q: What are the four stages of a change impact assessment, in order, per this lesson?
options: Propose, trace lineage, classify risk, sign off and communicate
Deploy, monitor, rollback, document
Design, build, test, deploy
Trace lineage, propose, deploy, review
questions.explain: The change is proposed precisely, lineage is traced and documented, the findings are risk-classified, and then the change is approved and communicated to affected owners before shipping.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why shouldn't risk classification be based purely on the number of downstream consumers found?
options: Because a change touching one Critical Data Element can be higher risk than a change touching several non-critical tables
Because risk classification is not useful for any kind of change
Because the number of consumers is always inaccurate
Because only upstream consumers matter for risk
questions.explain: Severity matters more than count — any trace that touches a CDE should be treated as at least medium risk, regardless of how small the trace otherwise looks.

questions.q: In the SalesFact grain-change example, which report got flagged high risk, and why?
options: The report counting rows as 'number of orders,' because changing the grain would make it silently double- or triple-count
All three SUM(Amount) reports, because grain changes always break aggregations
None of the reports, because grain changes never affect existing reports
The report with the most columns, because it is the most complex
questions.explain: The SUM(Amount) reports still aggregate correctly at the new grain, but the row-count report's logic assumed the old grain and would silently produce wrong counts.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a change impact assessment document capture at minimum?
options: What's changing, who's affected, a risk level, and a rollback plan
Only the name of the engineer who requested the change
The total storage cost of the affected tables
A list of every table in the database, regardless of relevance
questions.explain: Those four fields — what's changing, who's affected, risk level, and rollback plan — are the minimum content that makes the document actually useful.
